strengths: Ambitious and well-executed unification of many audio/music generation tasks (T2A, V2A, TV2A, T2M, V2M, TV2M, inpainting, music completion, zero-shot image-to-audio) within a single DiT framework, which is a meaningful step toward generalist audio models.

Strong empirical results across a broad set of benchmarks (AudioCaps, VGGSound, AVVP, MusicCaps, V2M-bench) with a comprehensive set of metrics (KL, IS, FD, FAD, PC/PQ, alignment) and comparisons against many recent baselines including MMAudio, Tango 2, and VidMuse.
Two sizeable curated caption datasets (vggsound-caps, V2M-caps) that address a genuine data bottleneck, with a clear annotation pipeline and a promise to open-source the caption data.

Useful ablations: mask ratios per modality, input vs. feature masking (with supporting analysis on information leakage), and unified vs. single-modality models, which substantiate the paper's main design claims.
Includes both automatic and subjective (user study) evaluations, plus qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the model is largely an assembly of existing components (CLIP-ViT, T5, Stable Audio Open autoencoder and pretrained DiT backbone) with simple input-level random masking; the masking idea is a straightforward application of well-known masked modeling techniques, and the technical description of the diffusion setup is standard.

Comparison fairness is a concern: AudioX is trained on substantially more data than most baselines (5.7M V2M captions, 175K private text-music pairs, multiple datasets), so SOTA results may reflect data scale rather than the architecture or masking strategy; the private portion of the training data also hurts reproducibility.

Caption quality from Qwen2-Audio is not validated (no human verification of the 190K/6M pseudo-captions), and hallucinated or generic captions could bias training; the effect of caption quality is not ablated.

Some claims are overstated relative to the tables (e.g., AudioX is not best on all metrics — alignment is worse than MMAudio on several V2A settings, and some V2M-bench margins are small), and no statistical significance or variance reporting is provided for any results; the user study is small (10 raters, 25 samples per task).

Potential evaluation circularity: VGGSound test evaluation uses captions from the same captioning pipeline applied to the same data distribution used in training, which may inflate text-conditioned metrics on VGGSound.

Several important details are missing or under-specified: how masking is handled at inference, how zero-padding for missing modalities interacts with classifier-free guidance, image-conditioning mechanics for the zero-shot image-to-audio result, and compute-fair baseline comparisons.
Ethics/licensing of the proprietary text-music data and copyright status of large-scale scraped music (V2M) are not discussed.

strengths: Broad task coverage: a single DiT-based model handles text/video/image/audio-to-audio, text/video-to-music, audio inpainting, and music completion, which is an attractive generalist capability for the audio domain.

Significant dataset contribution: two large caption corpora (vggsound-caps, V2M-caps) generated with an automated Qwen2-Audio pipeline, with plans to open-source them; this is useful for the community.
Extensive quantitative benchmarking across many tasks and baselines (MMAudio, Tango 2, Stable Audio Open, FoleyCrafter, VidMuse, etc.), including an out-of-domain evaluation on AVVP.
Ablations cover mask ratios per modality, input vs. feature masking, and unified vs. single-modality models, supporting the main design choice.
The paper is generally readable, with implementation details (model size, training compute, mask ratios, CFG scale) provided.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the model is largely a re-assembly of existing components (Stable Audio Open DiT, CLIP ViT, T5, audio autoencoder) with concatenation-based conditioning; the input-masking idea is a straightforward application of MAE-style masking, and the novelty gap over joint-training approaches like MMAudio is not clearly articulated.

Potential evaluation bias / contamination concerns: the test captions on VGGSound (and possibly MusicCaps-related data) come from the same automated captioning pipeline and caption distribution used in training, which can inflate CLAP-based alignment and distributional metrics relative to baselines evaluated with human/ground-truth captions; the relationship between training (e.g., V2M, MUCaps) and test splits (V2M-bench, MusicCaps) is not convincingly separated.

Claims are stronger than the evidence: 'achieves SOTA across most metrics' is only partially supported — MMAudio beats AudioX on several V2A/TV2A metrics (KL, FD, Align on VGGSound), and alignment on some tasks is actually lower than baselines; the abstract emphasizes IS, a known-unreliable metric, and Fig. 1's radar chart headline rests on it.

IS values on V2M-bench are near 1.3–1.5 for all methods, suggesting the metrics are close to degenerate in that regime, making fine-grained 'SOTA' distinctions on music tasks questionable; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.
The user study is very small (10 raters, 25 samples per task) with limited methodological detail, and no audio examples are verifiable from the text.

Inconsistencies in the paper: the abstract reports 190K/6M captions while Section 3.2 reports ~260K/5.7M; Table 4 is said to appear in the Appendix but is in the main text; Figure 5's y-axis and per-task breakdown are unclear; 'MUCaps' appears in training but is never defined.

Missing ablations and analysis: no comparison of inference cost vs. specialists, no analysis of failure modes, no discussion of how conflicting modalities are resolved, and the mask-strategy ablation (Table A3) is thin (single setting, small margins).

Data licensing and ethics are unaddressed: captions derived from large YouTube-scale corpora (V2M, VGGSound, AudioSet) and 'proprietary text-music pair data' raise copyright/consent questions that the paper does not discuss.

strengths: Ambitious unification: a single DiT-based model supporting text-, video-, image-, and audio-conditioned audio and music generation, plus inpainting and completion, evaluated across an unusually broad set of benchmarks (AudioCaps, VGGSound, AVVP, MusicCaps, V2M-bench).

Substantial data contribution: two large-scale caption datasets (vggsound-caps, ~190K; V2M-caps, ~6M) that are promised to be open-sourced, addressing a real scarcity of multi-modal paired data in audio generation.

Comprehensive quantitative evaluation with standard metrics (KL, IS, FD, FAD, PC/PQ, alignment) plus a user study, and comparison against many recent baselines including MMAudio, Tango 2, Stable Audio Open, and FoleyCrafter.
Useful ablations on mask ratios per modality, masking strategy (input vs. feature vs. none), and unified vs. single-modality models, which support the central design claims.
The paper is generally well organized and the method is clearly described, supporting reproducibility of the high-level approach.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach is essentially a DiT with concatenated frozen-encoder embeddings (CLIP, T5, audio autoencoder) plus an input-masking strategy borrowed from masked autoencoding (MAE/AudioMAE/VideoMAE). Masked multimodal joint training for audio has already been explored (e.g., MMAudio, MDSGen), so the technical contribution is incremental.

Evaluation fairness and potential circularity: the model is trained on Qwen2-Audio-generated captions for the same corpora (e.g., VGGSound) on which it is evaluated, while baselines are not given this data. The largest gains (e.g., IS 20.27 vs. 17.83 on VGGSound T2A) may partly reflect exposure to synthetic captions matched to the evaluation distribution rather than intrinsic modeling superiority.

Possible train/test contamination: Table A2 lists the 'AVVP Test Split' among annotated caption sources, raising a concern that AVVP test data or its captions were involved in training, which would undermine the out-of-domain AVVP claims.

Claims occasionally overstate the evidence: the model loses to MMAudio on several key metrics (e.g., V2A FD 8.83 vs. 6.18 on VGGSound; AVVP FD/FAD), and in image-to-audio its alignment (0.23) is far below Im2Wav (0.41), yet these are described as 'comparable' or 'excellent' without careful discussion.

Caption quality is never validated: synthetic captions from Qwen2-Audio are used wholesale; no human verification of caption accuracy/noise rates is reported, though caption noise directly affects both training and CLAP-based alignment metrics.
Reproducibility gaps: 175.2K clips of proprietary text-music data are used in training but cannot be released; the release URL is empty and the paper is marked 'work in progress.'
User study is small (10 raters, 25 samples per task) with no statistical significance testing; Figures 4 and 6 are hard to read, and Figure 5's axes/values are not clearly interpretable.
No variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-run results are reported for any experiment; single-seed numbers on generative metrics like FAD/IS can be noisy.

strengths: Strong and clearly motivated system contribution: AudioX unifies text-, video-, and audio-conditioned audio and music generation in a single DiT-based framework, and demonstrates competitive or SOTA results against specialist models across many tasks (T2A, V2A, TV2A, T2M, V2M) and datasets (AudioCaps, VGGSound, AVVP, MusicCaps, V2M-bench).

Substantial data contribution: the IF-caps dataset (~7M samples) with a structured two-stage annotation pipeline (Gemini 2.5 Pro for seed annotations, Qwen2-Audio for cost-effective augmentation) addresses a real bottleneck in unified audio generation, and the structured schema (category/count/SED/time-relation) is a thoughtful design that plausibly enables instruction-following.

Comprehensive evaluation including a new instruction-following benchmark (T2A-bench), the AudioTime benchmark, objective metrics (KL/IS/FD/FAD/PC/PQ/CLAP/ImageBind), and a human study with professional annotators; ablations cover both data curation sources and MAF architecture components.

The 'cross-modal regularization effect' finding — that higher-quality textual supervision improves non-text-conditioned tasks (V2A) under unified training — is an interesting empirical insight with practical implications.
The authors commit to open-sourcing captions, the benchmark, and code, and transparently disclose the use of LLMs in methodology and writing.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation circularity: Gemini 2.5 Pro is used to (a) generate the training captions, (b) author the T2A-bench prompts, and (c) serve as the automated judge for the benchmark's instruction-following metrics. A model trained on Gemini-style structured annotations may be favored by a Gemini judge; no independent validation of the judge's accuracy against human judgments is reported, and this weakens the headline claim of 'superior instruction-following'.

Reproducibility concerns: a large portion of music training data is 'Private' (175.2k clips, ~11.7k hours), and the V2M source data (5.7M clips) is not clearly redistributable; the paper does not discuss how the model or dataset can be fully reproduced. There is also no discussion of possible train/test overlap (e.g., V2M data used for both training and test splits of V2M/TV2M and music completion).

Limited architectural novelty: the MAF module (gating + cross-attention with learnable modality queries + self-attention with residual dispatch) is a fairly standard fusion recipe (Perceiver/Flamingo-style), and the overall framework is a DiT with cross-attention conditioning plus zero-padding for missing modalities; the gains shown in Table 4 are modest in absolute terms.

Benchmark validity details are thin: T2A-bench prompts are LLM-generated without reported human verification of ambiguity or answer-key correctness; strict exact-match metrics (e.g., exact count matching) on continuous or ambiguous sounds could be noisy, and the 1s tolerance window for timestamps is not justified.

Some results are uneven: e.g., on AVVP TV2A, AudioX trails MMAudio on most metrics, and on V2M V2A alignment (0.26) trails several baselines; the paper's blanket SOTA claims could be more carefully qualified. The user study is small (10 raters, 25 samples/task) and details on inter-rater agreement are absent.

Several important methodological details are relegated to the appendix or unclear in the main text (e.g., how the SED/time-relation supervision is converted into training captions, classifier-free guidance conditioning structure, VGGSound-caption augmentation effects), making it hard to assess the exact source of the instruction-following gains.

strengths: Ambitious and well-motivated goal: a single unified model supporting T2A, V2A, TV2A, T2M, V2M, audio inpainting, and music completion is a meaningful engineering contribution to the generalist-audio-model line of work.

Large-scale dataset contribution (IF-caps, ~7M samples) with a structured annotation schema (category/count, SED timestamps, time relations) and a two-stage annotation pipeline (Gemini 2.5 Pro + Qwen2-Audio augmentation), which the authors commit to open-sourcing.

Comprehensive breadth of evaluation: many tasks, many established metrics (KL, IS, FD, FAD, PC/PQ, CLAP, ImageBind), an out-of-domain test set (AVVP), a user study, and ablations on both data curation and the MAF module.
The paper is generally well written and clearly structured, with implementation details (backbone, encoders, optimizer, GPU hours, CFG scale) provided.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The framework is a fairly standard DiT with per-modality encoders and cross-attention conditioning. The MAF module is a lightweight combination of well-known components (gating, cross-attention with learnable queries/experts, self-attention, residual updates) that resembles existing gated/adapter-style fusion blocks; the paper does not articulate what is fundamentally new, and the gains from MAF in Table 4 are small (e.g., KL 1.69 -> 1.68, FAD 2.00 -> 1.98).

Serious circularity/confound in the central instruction-following claim. T2A-bench prompts are generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro, the benchmark is evaluated by Gemini 2.5 Pro as the judge, and AudioX is trained on IF-caps annotations produced by the very same Gemini 2.5 Pro pipeline. The model is therefore trained on the annotation distribution that both creates and scores the benchmark, making the large instruction-following margins in Table 2 difficult to attribute to genuine instruction-following ability rather than shared distribution/generator bias. This undermines the headline claim of the paper.

Baseline comparisons are confounded by data scale. AudioX (2.4B params) is trained on ~7M newly annotated multimodal samples (~36k hours) plus a 240s-clip private music corpus of ~11.7k hours, while baselines are trained on much smaller, different data. The claimed superiority cannot be attributed to the proposed method or framework rather than sheer data volume, and no controlled comparison (e.g., baselines trained on IF-caps) is provided. The 'cross-modal regularization effect' narrative is similarly only supported by correlational ablations.

Potential train/test contamination is not addressed. AudioCaps, VGGSound, and MusicCaps appear both as training sources (via IF-caps and captioning of those clips) and as test sets; Table A.1 does not make clear how test clips were excluded from the 1268k IF-caps training samples or from the private music data. Similarly, T2A-bench prompts derived from the same annotation vocabulary used in training are not tested against a held-out, human-written prompt set.

Evaluation protocol weaknesses: 250 inference steps with CFG 7.0 for the proposed model while baseline settings are not harmonized; Gemini-as-judge binary scoring for the new benchmark is validated only by qualitative examples and trend consistency, with no human-agreement study of the judge; the user study involves only 10 raters with 25 samples per task and no statistical significance testing.

The private music dataset (175.2k clips of 240s) lacks provenance, licensing, and copyright discussion, which is a notable omission for a paper releasing both the data and models; the ethics and broader-impact discussion is essentially absent.

Several results are presented without scrutiny: IS (chosen as the unified comparison metric) is a known unreliable metric for audio generation; 'SOTA or comparable' claims are glossed where the model actually loses to MMAudio on V2A (e.g., KL, Align.) and AVVP TV2A metrics; and Fig. 1 aggregates heterogeneous benchmarks via a single score with little justification.

strengths: Genuinely unified scope: a single model supports T2A, V2A, TV2A, T2M, V2M, TV2M, audio inpainting, and music completion, which is a meaningful step beyond single-task specialist models in audio generation.

Substantial data contribution: the IF-caps dataset (~7M samples with structured captions, SED timestamps, counts, and temporal relations) addresses a real bottleneck for unified multimodal audio training, and the two-stage annotation pipeline (Gemini 2.5 Pro seed + Qwen2-Audio augmentation) is a sensible cost/quality trade-off.

Comprehensive and well-organized evaluation: many tasks, many baselines categorized by input modality and output domain, both objective metrics (KL, IS, FD, FAD, PC/PQ, CLAP/ImageBind alignment) and a formal user study with professional evaluators, plus intra-/inter-modal ablations.

Ablation studies are thoughtful and support the two main claims: data curation strategy (Table 3) and MAF components (Table 4), including the interesting empirical observation of a cross-modal regularization effect.

Proposes T2A-bench with an automated two-step (blind annotation + judgment) evaluation pipeline for instruction-following, a currently under-measured capability, and commits to open-sourcing code, data, and benchmark.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core architecture is a DiT backbone largely reused from prior work (pretrained from Evans et al., 2024b) with standard encoders; the MAF module (gating + cross-attention with learnable queries + self-attention with residual updates) is a conventional fusion design with only 60M parameters, and its ablation gains are marginal (e.g., IS 11.84 vs 10.70 w/o MAF, with some metrics like Ordering slightly better without the Query component).

Potential circularity/bias in the instruction-following evaluation: T2A-bench prompts are generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro, judged by Gemini 2.5 Pro, and the model is trained on IF-caps captions produced by the same model family/distribution. The large instruction-following gains in Table 2 could partially reflect training/evaluation distribution match rather than genuine generalization; no out-of-distribution instruction set or human-verified benchmark subset is provided.

No statistical significance or variance reporting: key ablation differences (Tables 3-4) and baseline comparisons are small and reported without confidence intervals or repeated runs, making some conclusions (e.g., MAF component contributions) hard to trust.

The cross-modal regularization effect, presented as a notable finding, is supported only by one ablation configuration; alternative explanations (more diverse training captions increasing effective data volume) are not controlled for.

Reproducibility gaps: a large portion of the training data is private (175.2k clips of 240s music, ~11.7k hours), and code/datasets are only promised, not yet released; user study uses only 10 raters and 25 samples per task.

Some benchmark choices raise questions: IS is used as the headline unified comparison metric in Fig. 1 despite being a weak metric for audio quality, and on AVVP the model underperforms MMAudio on several metrics (FD, Align.) while the narrative emphasizes competitiveness.
